gifts.desc: You're first awake and first warm most mornings, and the day seems to open around you before anyone's had coffee. That part runs on its own. It's the people nearest you who notice first when the light dips.
There's more warmth in you than most days ask for, and you hand it out without checking who's earned it. Strangers get the same welcome regulars do. It hasn't run out yet.

The books you finished years ago, the odd skill you picked up on a whim, the friendships you actually paid attention to, all of it sits banked and unlit. Then on some ordinary morning it catches. What looks like a quick answer to everyone else took a decade to collect.
Whatever the week needs, there's fuel for it somewhere in what you've already read, tried, or lived through. The supply runs deep. You never show up with nothing to burn.
An excited idea doesn't stay a feeling for long around you. It gets written down, taught to someone, turned into the plan the group leans on every year after. It sticks.

The negotiation nobody else wants to run, or the skill that takes a year to earn, finally makes you feel like the day is using all of you. Simple errands barely register. An easy afternoon just leaves you restless.
You make the better call after someone asks one calm, unhurried question and lets the idea sit overnight before you act on it. The urge to leap gets tested first. It holds.

shadows.desc: Your evenings run hotter than they should, the mind still lit long after the day is supposedly done. Sleep shows up late. Even rest starts to feel like a task you're failing.
When you're fully lit, the conversation ends up about you, simply because you're the brightest thing around. Other people's ideas get harder to see next to that. You don't notice.

Another course gets bought, another book gets started, another plan gets drafted, none of it required before you could have simply begun. It burns hot for a week. Then it goes quiet, and most of what you gathered never gets used.
One good week of momentum and you'll spend months of saved-up energy on it, every book and contact and plan called in at once. The blaze looks great from outside. Nothing's left for the next season.

A passing thought gets a name, a folder, a launch date, before anyone's checked if it needed to exist past Tuesday. Everything you touch wants to become permanent. You're thinner by the time it's finished than you were when you started it.
The project shipped a month ago and you're still adjusting a line nobody else remembers is there. Settled things get reopened. Done turns out to be a decision you keep making twice.

A plan gets checked, then checked again, then checked once more, and by the third pass the moment that made it worth doing has quietly left. Every spark gets a hearing first. You end up being the hardest question you have to answer.
